topics: 💀 Sin Offerings That Died — why rabbinic me'ilah was needed even though people distance themselves from a dead sin offering
🐦 Rav Yosef's Proof — three mishnayot about bird offerings combine to refute Rabba
🏛️ Rabbi Elazar's Question — a personal-altar burnt offering brought into the Temple courtyard is 'absorbed' by its partitions
❓ Unresolved Dilemma — if that offering is later disqualified and ascends the altar, does it descend? Teiku
🚫 Rav Giddel's Rule — piggul intent at sprinkling and its effect on me'ilah for offerings of greater and lesser sanctity
📜 Rav Pappa's Challenge — the thanks-offering loaves prove piggul can create me'ilah, resolved by distinguishing slaughter from sprinkling

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Refining the Rules of Me'ilah
overview.subtitle: Meilah 3a–3b
overview.hebrewSource: זְרִיקַת פִּיגּוּל אֵינוֹ מוֹצִיא מִידֵי מְעִילָה בְּקׇדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים, וְאֵינוֹ מֵבִיא לִידֵי מְעִילָה בְּקָדָשִׁים קַלִּים
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf first explains why Ulla's rule about sacrificial animals that died was necessary even though a similar case (sin offerings left to die) was already known — the difference is whether people distance themselves from the animal during its lifetime or only afterward. Rav Yosef then marshals three mishnayot about disqualified bird offerings to conclusively refute Rabba's view that disqualified offerings must descend from the altar. The Gemara turns to Rabbi Elazar's teaching that a personal-altar offering brought into the Temple courtyard is 'absorbed' by its partitions, and his unresolved dilemma about whether such an offering, if later disqualified, must descend from the altar. The daf closes with Rav Giddel's rule about piggul intent during blood-sprinkling and its effect on me'ilah, tested against a mishna about the thanks offering's loaves.

slides.title: 💀 Two Kinds of 'Distancing' From a Dead Offering
slides.subtitle: Why the Sages needed Ulla's rule even for ordinary sacrificial animals that died
rows: Sin offering disqualified while alive (e.g. its owner atoned differently)
Yes, already in its lifetime — it looks unfit
No decree needed — no one benefits from it anyway
Sin offering fit in life, then dies
No — it looked fine until it died
Decree needed to stop casual misuse
Other offerings of the most sacred order that die
No — not brought for atonement, so people assume no reason to avoid them
Ulla's decree: still needed, since they look like valid offerings

callout.label: The logic:
callout.text: Rabbinic me'ilah is instituted precisely where people would NOT naturally avoid a disqualified offering — since it still looks legitimate, a decree is needed to prevent casual misuse.

slides.title: 🐦 Rav Yosef's Three-Mishna Proof Against Rabba
slides.subtitle: Chaining sources to show a disqualified offering that ascended the altar does not descend

steps.content: 1️⃣ Mishna (Zevaḥim 66b): bird offerings disqualified by wrong-place rites don't impurify the throat when swallowed, and ARE subject to me'ilah
2️⃣ Mishna (Zevaḥim 68b): 'whose disqualification occurred in the sacred area' likewise doesn't impurify the throat — so the first mishna's birds are cases of disqualification 'in the sacred area'
3️⃣ Mishna (Zevaḥim 84a): anything disqualified 'in the sacred area' — if it ascended the altar, it does NOT descend
4️⃣ Combine all three: these birds, disqualified in the sacred area, are subject to me'ilah AND do not descend if they ascended
5️⃣ תְּיוּבְתָּא — conclusive refutation of Rabba, who held disqualified offerings must always descend

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: Rav Yosef wins this exchange: an offering disqualified inside the Temple courtyard, once it ascends the altar, stays there — supporting his view that the mishna's me'ilah could be Torah-law, not merely rabbinic.

slides.title: 🏛️ Rabbi Elazar's Dilemma: A Personal Altar's Offering in the Temple
slides.subtitle: What happens when an offering meant for a private bamah enters the Temple courtyard?

lines.speaker: R' Elazar
lines.text: קְלָטוּהָ מְחִיצוֹת לְכׇל דָּבָר — a burnt offering consecrated for a personal altar that one brought into the Temple courtyard is 'absorbed' by the courtyard's partitions for every purpose, taking on full Temple-offering status.

lines.speaker: R' Elazar asks
lines.text: If that offering is then disqualified — say, slaughtered in the south — and its limbs ascend the altar, what is the halakha: do they descend?

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Perhaps even Rabba would agree here they descend only if the owner intended to sacrifice it properly within the courtyard; had he intended a personal altar, slaughtering in the south wouldn't fully disqualify it, so it stays.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Or perhaps even Rav Yosef would agree it descends here — since it was never properly admitted by the courtyard's partitions in the first place, unlike an offering consecrated for the Temple.

callout.label: Note:
callout.text: Rabbi Elazar's second question is asked 'one dilemma from another' — it doesn't reveal which side of the Rabba/Rav Yosef debate he holds for the standard case.

slides.title: 🚫 Rav Giddel's Rule: Piggul Intent at Sprinkling
slides.subtitle: The blood-sprinkling stage governs whether piggul removes or creates me'ilah

boxes.title: Offerings of the Most Sacred Order
items: Piggul intent at sprinkling does NOT remove the meat from me'ilah
Reason: no valid sprinkling ever permitted the priests to eat it
It remains 'the sacred items of the Lord' (Leviticus 5:15)

boxes.title: Offerings of Lesser Sanctity
items: Piggul intent at sprinkling does NOT bring the sacrificial portions into me'ilah
Only a VALID sprinkling confers me'ilah status on lesser offerings
Without proper sprinkling, no me'ilah applies to them at all

callout.label: Rav Giddel said Rav said:
callout.text: In both directions, an invalid (piggul) sprinkling changes nothing about me'ilah — sacred-order offerings stay subject to it, lesser offerings stay exempt from it.

slides.title: 📜 Rav Pappa's Objection From the Thanks-Offering Loaves
slides.subtitle: Does piggul at slaughter alone create me'ilah for offerings of lesser sanctity?

nodes.content: ❓ Mishna (Menaḥot 78b): thanks offering slaughtered chutz lizmano/limkomo — the loaves ARE sanctified and subject to me'ilah
⚡ Rav Pappa to Abaye: this contradicts Rav Giddel — piggul intent DOES bring lesser-sanctity offerings into me'ilah! Abaye is silent.
💡 Rabbi Abba's resolution: the mishna's piggul intent was at slaughter only, not at sprinkling — sprinkling was proper, so me'ilah applies normally
🔄 Rav Ashi challenges Rava: but Ulla says a piggul handful (komeitz) burned on the altar loses its piggul status — and komeitz = slaughter!
✅ Rava: Ulla meant only a prohibited act occurred, not full piggul — full piggul status still needs improper intent at the offering-up stage too

callout.label: Bottom line:
callout.text: Piggul intent limited to the slaughter stage, without matching intent at sprinkling, does not remove an offering from ordinary me'ilah rules.

summary.principle: Rabbinic me'ilah is decreed precisely where people would not naturally distance themselves from a disqualified offering, and piggul status only fully controls an offering's me'ilah when the improper intent spans both slaughter and the permitting rite (sprinkling or offering-up).

flowSteps.content: 💀 Why decree me'ilah on animals that died? Only where people wouldn't naturally avoid them
🐦 Rav Yosef's three-mishna chain: disqualified-in-the-courtyard birds don't descend from the altar — refutes Rabba

columns.content: 🏛️ R' Elazar: personal-altar offering absorbed by Temple partitions — but if later disqualified, teiku on descent
🚫 R' Giddel: piggul at sprinkling never changes an offering's baseline me'ilah status

flowSteps.content: 📜 Loaves of the thanks offering: piggul intent at slaughter alone still allows normal me'ilah
🎓 Key Principle: full piggul status — and its effect on me'ilah — requires improper intent at BOTH slaughter and the permitting rite

quiz.q: Why did Ulla's rule about sacrificial animals of the most sacred order that die need to be stated separately, even though a similar rule about dead sin offerings was already known?
o: Because sin offerings are never subject to me'ilah
Because people distance themselves from a sin offering that died in a way they don't for other offerings that die, so a separate decree was needed
Because sin offerings are more expensive
Because the two cases are actually identical and no new teaching was needed
quiz.e: Sin offerings that die look unfit only after death (they looked fine in life), while other sacred-order offerings that die still look legitimate, requiring a distinct decree so people don't casually misuse them.

quiz.q: How does Rav Yosef combine three mishnayot about disqualified bird offerings to refute Rabba?
o: He shows birds are never subject to me'ilah
He chains the mishnayot to show that offerings disqualified in the sacred area, once they ascend the altar, do not descend — contradicting Rabba
He proves that bird offerings cannot be piggul
He shows that Rabba never actually held his stated opinion
quiz.e: By linking the three mishnayot, Rav Yosef shows these birds are 'disqualified in the sacred area' and that such offerings do not descend once they ascend — a conclusive refutation (teyuvta) of Rabba.

quiz.q: What does Rabbi Elazar teach about a burnt offering consecrated for a personal altar (bamat yaḥid) that is brought into the Temple courtyard?
o: It becomes disqualified immediately
It is 'absorbed' by the courtyard's partitions and takes on full Temple-offering status
It must be redeemed for money
It can never be sacrificed anywhere
quiz.e: Rabbi Elazar teaches that the Temple courtyard's partitions 'admit' such an offering for all purposes, giving it the status of a regular Temple offering from that point on.

quiz.q: According to Rav Giddel citing Rav, what effect does piggul intent during blood-sprinkling have on offerings of lesser sanctity?
o: It always subjects them to me'ilah
It never brings their sacrificial portions into the status of being subject to me'ilah, since only a valid sprinkling confers that status
It exempts them from all sacrificial law
It has no effect because lesser offerings can never become piggul
quiz.e: Rav Giddel taught that only a valid (non-piggul) sprinkling brings offerings of lesser sanctity into the category of me'ilah; piggul intent at sprinkling does not create that status.

quiz.q: How does Rabbi Abba resolve Rav Pappa's objection from the mishna about the thanks offering's loaves (which are subject to me'ilah when the offering was slaughtered chutz lizmano/limkomo)?
o: He says the mishna is not authoritative
He distinguishes: the mishna's piggul intent was only at slaughter, not at sprinkling, so normal me'ilah rules still apply
He says loaves are never subject to me'ilah
He says the thanks offering is not really an offering of lesser sanctity
quiz.e: Rabbi Abba explains that Rav Giddel's rule concerns piggul intent specifically at sprinkling; the mishna's case involved piggul intent only at slaughter, with proper sprinkling, so the loaves remain subject to ordinary me'ilah.
